records.excerpt: The week’s defining asset-based lending story was a take-private built on a classic borrowing base. Utz Brands closed its Intersnack transaction on November 20 with an amended and restated $250 million senior secured ABL revolver agented by Bank of America and arranged by a seven-bank group, priced at Term SOFR plus 175 basis points on an availability grid and sitting alongside a $1.1 billion term loan.1,2 The receivables market moved just as fast: Avnet lifted its Wells Fargo-agented securitization to $1.2 billion from $700 million, C.H. Robinson moved its $750 million program’s agency from Bank of America to Wells Fargo and extended it to 2028, and Nabors loosened eligibility in its receivables purchase facility even as it cut the limit to $200 million.4,5,6 At the stressed end, White Oak repriced Lulu’s Fashion Lounge to SOFR plus 450 in exchange for overformula room, seasonal inventory advances and a Gordon Brothers monitoring requirement.8 The macro backdrop turned violent. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 10% for the week and the S&P 500 dropped roughly 8.6% to 6,910.39 after an AI and semiconductor unwind, while the 2-year and 10-year Treasury yields each fell about 19 basis points to roughly 4.65% and 4.94%.31,33 The Fed did not blink: October minutes showed “almost all participants” expect further hikes, Governor Christopher Waller argued for a 50-basis-point move in December, and CME FedWatch priced a December increase from the current 3.75%–4.00% range as a near-certainty.24,26,29,30 For middle market lenders, a widening high-yield spread and rising floating-rate costs make availability-based structures, springing covenants and collateral monitoring the decisive tools heading into year-end. Bank of America Anchors Utz’s $250 Million Take-Private ABL at SOFR+175 With a Seven-Bank Group Utz Brands amended and restated its ABL credit agreement on November 20 in connection with the closing of its take-private by Intersnack. The facility provides up to $250 million of senior secured revolving commitments, with $12 million drawn at close, a $30 million accordion and a maturity of November 20, 2031.1,2 Bank of America serves as administrative and collateral agent, with BNP Paribas, Deutsche Bank, Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo as joint lead arrangers; the revolver sits beside a $1.1 billion Bank of America-agented term loan maturing in 2033.1,2 Pricing opens at Term SOFR plus 1.75% and then moves on an average-excess-availability grid from SOFR plus 1.50% (above 66.7% availability) to SOFR plus 2.00% (below 33.3%), with an unused fee of 0.375%–0.50%.2 The borrowing base advances 85% against eligible receivables — 90% for account debtors rated Baa3/BBB- or better, stepping to 92.5% during a four-month seasonal window — plus inventory at the lesser of a cost rate and an NOLV rate, eligible cash at 100%, and real estate at 60% of a $94.38 million appraisal, capped at the lesser of $50 million and 30% of the line cap, with the 60% advance rate stepping down one percentage point per quarter beginning March 31, 2027.2 The only maintenance-style test is a springing 1.00x fixed charge coverage ratio, triggered when excess availability falls below the greater of 10% of the line cap or $25 million.2 Executive Chairman Dylan Lissette called the closing “the beginning of an important new chapter for Utz.”3 For asset-based lenders, the structure is a template for sponsor-style take-privates of branded consumer companies: a rating-sensitive receivables advance, a seasonal kicker for snack-food working capital, and a real estate component that self-liquidates — all governed by availability rather than leverage. Receivables Finance Takes Center Stage: Avnet Goes to $1.2 Billion, C.H. Robinson Switches Agents, Nabors Rewrites Eligibility Avnet signed Amendment No. 10 to its receivables purchase agreement on November 17, raising the maximum purchase limit to $1.2 billion from $700 million with Wells Fargo as agent and other terms “substantially the same.”4 A day later, C.H. Robinson amended its $750 million securitization, moving the administrative agent role from Bank of America to Wells Fargo, rebalancing commitments to $450 million from Wells Fargo and $300 million from Bank of America, and extending the scheduled termination to November 17, 2028; the same filing disclosed a $500 million U.S. Bank-agented senior unsecured delayed-draw term loan tied to the RXO acquisition.5 Nabors Industries moved the other way on size but loosened structure. Its Wells Fargo-agented receivables purchase facility was cut to $200 million from $250 million, with a one-time option to request up to $50 million more, while BOKF joined and Arab Banking Corp. exited.6 The amendment removed the 0.10% credit spread adjustment, raised the cross-aging threshold to 50% from 35%, allowed specified investment-grade obligors payment terms up to 90 days, and raised the unbilled-receivables concentration limit to 35% from 30%.6 In specialty finance, Enova amended its Truist-agented OnDeck asset-backed revolver to $365.1 million, with Class A notes at SOFR plus 1.30% on a 76% advance and Class B at SOFR plus 6.00%, for a blended SOFR plus 2.14% and a 92.5% total advance rate through a November 2028 revolving period.7 For secured lenders, the week shows that large-cap borrowers are leaning on receivables programs rather than unsecured revolvers as base rates climb. Middle market ABL lenders competing for distribution and logistics credits should expect borrowers to benchmark against these eligibility concessions — longer terms for investment-grade obligors, looser cross-aging and higher unbilled concentrations. records.title: Ackman Takes Aim at Fed's Inflation Target, Calls 3% More Realistic and Warns Another Rate Hike Would Trigger Global Recession
records.excerpt: Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman posted on social media questioning the legitimacy of the U.S. Federal Reserve's rigid adherence to a 2% inflation target, arguing that with financial conditions significantly tightened, 3% is a more realistic level. Citing SpaceX's recent secured debt financing rate of 8.259%—far above the under-6% rate on its unsecured bonds at IPO—he illustrated that corporate financing costs have climbed markedly, and warned that if the Fed hikes again at its December 9 meeting, it could push the U.S. and global economy into recession. Markets still expect a better-than-90% probability of a quarter-point hike in December, while within the Fed, Governor Cook leads the camp prioritizing inflation control.

Sections Home News & Events Press Releases Press Release November 20, 2026 Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. "I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations. For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955. Last Update: November 20, 2026

records.title: Stock market today: Dow futures jump 800 points and Nasdaq soars 3% after entering correction
records.excerpt: Investors are poised to begin a short trading week with some early holiday cheer after suffering the worst loss in more than six years. Investors are poised to begin a short trading week with some early holiday cheer after suffering the worst loss in more than six years. Recommended Video Futures tied to the Dow Jones industrial average surged 798 points, or 1.66%. S&P 500 futures shot up 2.11%, and Nasdaq futures soared 2.75%. That came after the Dow and Nasdaq notched their biggest weekly declines since the early days of the COVID-10 pandemic, while the S&P 500 saw its steepest such drop since April 2025, when President Donald Trump stunned markets with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The S&P 500 and Dow joined the Nasdaq in correction territory. Tech shares have led the selloff as Wall Street fears the AI boom is about to go bust. The downtrend began after the midterm elections handed victories to Democrats more skeptical of data centers. But the Nvidia spy scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s ouster as CEO poured more fuel on the fire, igniting additional worries that his “circular” financing deals would unravel and leave neocloud companies in its ecosystem without capital for new data centers or AI chips. In addition, revelations that China had backdoor access to high-end U.S. chips used in AI development are spurring a federal crackdown to close loopholes in export restrictions. Trump even vowed to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad. Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi warned in a social media post that the stock market selloff could weigh on economic growth via the wealth effect, which affects consumer spending. He estimated that that consumer spending rises or falls by about 2 cents for every $1 increase or decrease in net worth over about a year. That means that if stock prices stay where they are, the wealth effect will subtract almost 0.3 percentage points from real GDP growth a year from now, after adding 0.7 percentage points in this quarter. “We’ve seen AI stocks selloff before, only for them to rebound quickly. Investors have been conditioned to buy on the dip,” Zandi wrote. “But while there are sure to be lots of ups and downs in stock prices in the days ahead, it feels increasingly like the easy money in the AI trade has been made. If so, the economy won’t be able to count on AI to be the sole engine of growth.” But the end of the year also tends to lighten the mood on Wall Street and lift stocks. While the traditional “Santa Claus rally” is still weeks away, the upcoming shortened week could provide some early relief. Markets will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday and open for just a half day on Friday. Thin trading volumes could also amplify stock rebounds. Meanwhile, Wall Street forecasters remain upbeat about 2027 even as markets are in corrections. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs expect the S&P 500 to finish next year at 8,700. Meanwhile, UBS Global Wealth Management and Wells Fargo see 8,200. Then there’s Steve Chiavarone, chief investment officer for equities at Federated Hermes, who has a year-end view of 10,000—or a 45% surge from current levels. He brushed aside this month’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep Congress and several state capitals. While Wall Street fears the blue tsunami will slow the AI infrastructure boom, Chiavarone said risks to the buildout are overblown. Even a slight retreat would be positive. “A modest pullback in the data center buildout could give cash flows time to catch up, easing inflation pressures and making the investment boom more sustainable,” he argued. The show transforms Fortune ’s trusted reporting into actionable, conversational, and entertaining insights for an emerging class of business leaders. Watch here.

records.excerpt: Title: Senior Leader of the Sinaloa Cartel and One of FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives Arrested in Mexico Following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation URL Source: http://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/senior-leader-sinaloa-cartel-and-one-fbis-ten-most-wanted-fugitives-arrested-mexico Final URL: https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/senior-leader-sinaloa-cartel-and-one-fbis-ten-most-wanted-fugitives-arrested-mexico Published Time: 2026-11-21T18:08:42-05:00 Markdown Content: [Fausto Isidro Meza Flores](https://www.fbi.gov/wanted/topten/fausto-isidro-meza-flores?utm_medium=email&utm_source=govdelivery), also known as “Chapo Isidro,” an alleged leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, has been captured by the Mexican military following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation. “We commend Mexico’s military and special forces on last night’s capture of Sinaloa Cartel senior leader ‘Chapo Isidro,’ said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “A combined interagency effort, including the Homeland Security Task Force, supported this Mexican operation to remove a leader of one of the most dangerous drug cartels in Mexico. This successful operation is the result of a bilateral effort to eliminate terrorists in Mexico. We extend our condolences to the families of the elite soldiers who were killed and our gratitude to the Mexican government.” “The arrest of Chapo Isidro demonstrates the outstanding strength and reach of the Homeland Security Task Force,” said Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. “Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and our HSTF partners relentlessly pursued one of the world’s most dangerous cartel leaders, whose organization is alleged to have flooded our communities with deadly narcotics and terrorized communities through extreme violence. This operation sends an unmistakable message, cartel leaders cannot hide behind borders, money, or brutality. The Homeland Security Task Force will continue its work to dismantle these criminal and terrorist networks, hold their leaders accountable, and protect the American people.” Meza Flores was captured on November 20 in a spectacular military operation in Guasave, Sinaloa, Mexico, that also resulted in the arrest of alleged cartel leader German Rolando Galvez Meza, also known as “El Serafin.” A federal grand jury in the District of Columbia returned a second superseding indictment on September 25 charging Meza-Flores, 44, of Sonora, Mexico, with conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, conducting a continuing criminal enterprise, money laundering and firearms related charges. The case is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California and the Justice Department’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section. The Sinaloa Cartel is one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities. On February 20, 2025, the U.S. Secretary of State designated the Cartel de Sinaloa as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) under Section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act and as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist under Executive Order 13224.The Secretary of State has also listed the following aliases for the Cartel de Sinaloa: Sinaloa Cartel, Mexican Federation, and Guadalajara Cartel. According to court documents, under Meza Flores’s leadership, the Sinaloa Cartel produced and trafficked multi-tonnage quantities of drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl into the United States, and used extreme violence to further its operations. Meza Flores commanded a large contingent of gunmen to control significant territory in the Guasave, Los Mochis, and remote Sinaloa mountains. The cartel uses this territory to manufacture and distribute illicit controlled substances, transporting them north to the United States. It is further alleged that Meza Flores has engaged in continual and extreme violence, including (1) murdering rival cartel members in public; (2) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering rival cartel members at camps and elsewhere; (3) kidnapping, torturing, and murdering members of the Mexican police; and (4) terrorizing the people of Mexico. “Meza Flores is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives List for a reason; he is the most dangerous man in Mexico,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa Cartel, promoting unparalleled violence throughout southern Mexico and flooding the United States with deadly substances all in the name of profit. With this indictment made possible by the Homeland Security Task Force, subsequent arrest and the continued support of our Mexican partners, we aim to bring him to justice and fully dismantle this cartel.” “Chapo Isidro built an empire in the shadows. Today’s sunrise was his sunset,” said U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon for the Southern District of California. “Another FBI Ten Most Wanted fugitive is off the board,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” has been captured by Mexican forces with U.S. assistance. This alleged cartel leader is accused of flooding American communities with deadly drugs, including fentanyl. This is the 11th Ten Most Wanted fugitive captured under the Trump Administration. Outstanding work by our law enforcement partners in Mexico and everyone involved in this operation. Under President Trump’s leadership, this FBI will continue relentlessly pursuing the criminals and cartels poisoning our communities and threatening American lives.” “Homeland Security Investigations is proud of the exceptional work of our special agents and personnel across our domestic and international offices whose determination, expertise, and coordination through the HSTF helped bring Chapo Isidro to justice,” said HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Working alongside our HSTF partners, HSI investigated this dangerous cartel leader and helped dismantle the criminal enterprise he allegedly used to poison American communities and fuel brutal violence. This arrest demonstrates the reach of HSI’s global investigative authorities and the strength of the HSTF as partners work together to take coordinated and relentless action against transnational criminal organizations that threaten our homeland.” Meza Flores is charged in a six-count superseding indictment filed in the District of Columbia with leading a continuing criminal enterprise, conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and fentanyl for importation into the United States, international money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to provide material support to a terrorist organization, narcoterrorism, and using a firearm including a machinegun and a destructive device. If convicted of these charges, Meza Flores faces the death penalty or a mandatory term of life in prison. The U.S. Department of State is offering a reward of up to $5 million for information that led to the arrest and/or will lead to the conviction of Chapo Isidro. records.title: 'The 2% inflation ambition is misguided': Bill Ackman urges Fed to rethink policy
records.excerpt: Billionaire investor Bill Ackman warned that the Federal Reserve risks making “another mistake” at its December 9 meeting, arguing that financial conditions have tightened significantly and that the central bank should reconsider its 2% inflation target.In a post on X on Sunday, the Pershing Square… 'The 2% inflation ambition is misguided': Bill Ackman urges Fed to rethink policy 1 min read SPCX QQQ IEF SHY Billionaire investor Bill Ackman warned that the Federal Reserve risks making “another mistake” at its December 9 meeting, arguing that financial conditions have tightened significantly and that the central bank should reconsider its 2% inflation target. In a post on X on Sunday, the Pershing Square CEO said financial conditions have "tightened massively," pointing to SpaceX's SPCX recent secured debt financing at an 8.259% interest rate, compared with below 6% for its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO, as an example of rising corporate borrowing costs. He also said the substantial recent decline in the stock market has materially increased the cost of equity capital, adding to the pressure on businesses seeking financing. Ackman argued that the Fed's 2% inflation ambition is “misguided” given structural changes in the global economy, including geopolitical risks, higher military spending, deglobalization, tariffs, and massive investment in AI infrastructure and related energy capacity. "3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world," Ackman said, warning that further rate increases in an attempt to bring inflation down to 2% could push the U.S. and global economies into recession. His comments echo concerns raised by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has also cautioned the Fed against overtightening. "Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they overtighten," Bessent said, pointing to a substantial tightening in financial conditions over recent months. However, Fed officials have continued to emphasize the need to address persistent inflation. Fed Governor Lisa Cook has warned that the current policy rate may not be sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation under control, arguing that policymakers cannot afford to delay action. Meanwhile, minutes from the Fed's October 27-28 meeting showed that almost all policymakers considered further rate increases likely appropriate under their baseline outlook, although most supported holding rates steady at that meeting. CME Group interest-rate futures now price roughly a 95.2% probability of a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike next month, down from near certainty, with traders betting on a shorter tightening cycle. However, economists at several institutions argue that years of stock market gains far outweigh recent losses, and that short-term volatility is unlikely to sway policymakers. Markets are also watching for a reversal in AI optimism and the risk of shrinking household equity wealth.

records.title: Could Another Fed Rate Hike Be A Policy Mistake? Bill Ackman Says 3% Inflation Target Is More Realistic
records.excerpt: The Federal Reserve is set to meet in December for its last policy decision of 2026, with markets overwhelmingly expecting a rate hike after policymakers raised concerns about rising inflation.However, some Wall Street experts, including Pershing Square Inc.’s (PS) Bill Ackman, believe that a hike… Could Another Fed Rate Hike Be A Policy Mistake? Bill Ackman Says 3% Inflation Target Is More Realistic 3 min read QQQ TLT PS SPCX Key points: Data from the CME FedWatch tool puts the odds of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December at 93.2%, while the probability of holding rates steady is at 6.8%. According to Ackman, 3% inflation is a more realistic target. Economist James E. Thorne backed Ackman’s stance in a post on X. The Federal Reserve is set to meet in December for its last policy decision of 2026, with markets overwhelmingly expecting a rate hike after policymakers raised concerns about rising inflation. However, some Wall Street experts, including Pershing Square Inc.’s (PS) Bill Ackman, believe that a hike would be a policy mistake under current circumstances. Ackman Says Fed’s 2% Inflation Target Is ‘Misguided’ In a post on X, the activist investor said that he thinks the central bank is “about to make another mistake on December 9th” if it hikes interest rates under massively tightening financial conditions. He noted that the cost of equity capital has increased materially, even as there has been a recent decline in the stock market. Ackman highlighted the example of SpaceX (SPCX) , saying that the investment-grade company had recently raised secured debt financing at an 8.259% interest rate versus significantly below 6% for its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO. He also said that the Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. “Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, de-globalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set.” As per the hedge fund manager, 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition. “The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%,” he said. Thorne, Schiff Back Ackman’s Stance Apart from Ackman, other Wall Street economists have also raised concerns about the Fed potentially increasing its benchmark interest rate. Economist James E. Thorne backed Ackman’s stance, saying in a post on X that, “Yes, the Fed is about to make another policy mistake.” Data from the CME FedWatch tool puts the odds of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December at 93.2%, while the probability of holding rates steady is at 6.8%. Thorne said in a separate post, “Central bankers treat 2% inflation as a scientific constant. It is a policy choice, not a law of economics.” He argued that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s complaint that inflation has not reached 2% is a goal set by the Fed. In the meantime, services inflation has exceeded that rate 95% of the time over the past 60 years. “The target is not sacred. Another choice by central bankers not supported by theory or facts,” he added. Meanwhile, economist Peter Schiff posited that the Fed knows it cannot deliver the rate hikes necessary to return inflation to 2% without creating a financial crisis. “So the Fed threatens to hike, crashing stocks and commodities, which raises the odds of a recession, giving it an excuse not to hike,” he said. How Are Markets Reacting? The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) , which tracks the S&P 500 index, gained more than 1% in the overnight session late Sunday after slumping more than 8.5% last week. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bearish’ at the time of writing. One user said, “$SPY Lets not forget that every bull cycle has ended when the Fed has started a tightening cycle. And Now the Fed is under Chair Warsh, the most hawkish chair since Volker days. This is not the time to be invested in stocks, I’m speaking from facts.” The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) also edged higher in the overnight session, with sentiment in the ‘extremely bullish’ and ‘neutral’ territories, respectively. Another user said, “$QQQ The Fed just took margin away. Everyone that was leveraged just got smoked from all sectors. Now the fed can buy cheap gold and force deflation. Dollar got a lot stronger over the past month. Not the bottom but a lot of risk has been priced into the market. Know what you own and don’t over leverage. Governments made a deal after 2008 to never let the market go down again and I don’t think that has changed. This has been the most controlled calculated crash so far. Deflation is a lot scarier than inflation so I doubt that they can push this down for long.” The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was down 0.44% amid ‘bullish’ sentiment. records.title: Dietary Selenium Boosts Growth in Nile Tilapia Fed Low-Protein Plant-Oil Diets
records.excerpt:
In intensive aquaculture production, dietary protein represents one of the single most influential determinants of both overall feed expenditure and juvenile fish growth rates. Because fish rely heavily on balanced nutrient intake rather than crude protein concentration alone, aquaculture nutritionists have increasingly examined how non-protein dietary energy sources might spare dietary protein without compromising animal performance. In a controlled 56-day feeding experiment evaluating juvenile Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), researchers determined that supplementing practical reduced-protein diets with sodium selenite markedly improved growth metrics, enhanced feed utilisation, and stimulated somatic protein retention across several distinct plant-oil regimes. The study focused specifically on diets formulated to contain 28 percent crude protein, pairing them with vegetable lipid sources that differed substantially in fatty-acid chain length and degree of unsaturation.

To contextualise the nutritional challenge, previous meta-analyses and experimental trials in Nile tilapia have established that protein and energy sources interact directly to dictate nutrient partitioning, overall feed efficiency, and final carcass composition. Dietary lipids serve as vital sources of non-protein energy and indispensable fatty acids, yet the physiological responses of fish depend closely on total inclusion rates and specific fatty-acid profiles. Although Nile tilapia readily utilise various plant-derived oils, distinct lipid sources can alter digestive processes, tissue deposition, and systemic lipid metabolism. Virgin coconut oil, cold-extracted from Cocos nucifera, is dominated by medium-chain saturated fatty acids such as lauric acid, whereas candlenut oil, obtained from Aleurites moluccanus kernels, is characterised by high proportions of unsaturated oleic and linoleic acids. While both oils offer potential non-protein energy, their combined physiological interactions with essential trace minerals in reduced-protein diets had not been systematically evaluated under factorial conditions.

Alongside non-protein energy sources, selenium represents an indispensable micronutrient that incorporates directly into functional selenoproteins responsible for physiological redox regulation and cellular antioxidant defense. In farmed aquatic species, biological responses to dietary selenium depend rigorously on the animal's developmental life stage, baseline dietary trace mineral levels, the chemical form administered, and the absolute ingested concentration. Prior studies in juvenile tilapia demonstrated that growth outcomes, tissue deposition, and gut architecture vary substantially depending on whether selenium is provided in organic, inorganic, or particulate forms. Consequently, precise evaluations of selenium supplementation require measuring analysed total elemental concentrations in the finished feed rather than relying exclusively on nominal formulation values.

The experimental trial was conducted using 640 juvenile Nile tilapia with an initial average body weight of 10.2 plus or minus 0.4 grams, managed under an institutional animal ethics protocol and reported in reference to ARRIVE 2.0 guidelines. The juveniles were stratified by individual mass and randomly assigned across 32 glass aquaria, each maintaining a working volume of 45 to 50 litres with continuous aeration, dechlorinated freshwater exchanges of roughly 30 percent daily, and a standard 12-hour light and 12-hour dark cycle. Four independent replicate tanks, each stocking 20 fish, were allocated to each experimental diet. The trial was structured around an orthogonal three-by-two factorial design comparing three distinct 4 percent added-oil regimes against two selenium levels, accompanied by two non-factorial reference diets that supplied operational context without confounding the primary balanced statistical comparisons.

The factorial diets were formulated to remain isonitrogenous at 28 percent crude protein and approximately isoenergetic by balancing carbohydrate-bearing ingredients alongside a uniform 4 percent total added lipid content. These diets contrasted three oil regimes comprising a one-to-one blend of 2 percent virgin coconut oil and 2 percent candlenut oil, 4 percent virgin coconut oil alone, or 4 percent candlenut oil alone. Each lipid matrix was evaluated either without supplemental selenium, reflecting basal levels, or with nominal supplementation of 0.50 milligrams of selenium per kilogram of feed supplied as sodium selenite. Triplicate proximate analyses verified that the manufactured factorial diets contained between 28.08 and 28.12 percent crude protein and 9.15 to 9.22 percent crude lipid on a dry-matter basis. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry confirmed clear elemental separation, recording 0.16 to 0.17 milligrams of selenium per kilogram in unsupplemented feeds and 0.66 to 0.68 milligrams per kilogram in supplemented batches.

Two additional standalone control diets were formulated without supplemental oil or selenium to benchmark the nutritional performance of the factorial series. The first was an unsupplemented 28 percent crude-protein reference diet containing 5.35 percent crude lipid and 0.16 milligrams of selenium per kilogram, while the second was an unsupplemented 32 percent crude-protein reference diet providing 5.30 percent crude lipid and 0.18 milligrams of selenium per kilogram. The authors stressed that because these reference diets varied across multiple nutritional dimensions, including calculated energy densities and ingredient inclusion rates, contrasts involving them cannot establish isolated causal effects of oil supplementation or protein concentration. Instead, robust inferential conclusions were drawn from two-way analysis of variance across the six factorial treatments, treating each aquarium tank as an independent experimental unit.

Fish were fed to apparent satiation three times daily for 56 consecutive days, with feed intake recorded rigorously at each feeding event by recovering, drying, and weighing uneaten pellets to quantify dry-matter consumption. Overall survival remained remarkably high across all treatments, ranging from 96.25 to 98.75 percent with no significant differences among dietary regimes. Factorial analysis revealed that selenium supplementation exerted a highly significant positive main effect on final body weight and specific growth rate, with both endpoints reaching significance at p less than 0.001. In contrast, neither the main effect of the oil regime nor the interaction between oil source and selenium exerted a statistically significant influence on body weight gain or specific growth rate, indicating that sodium selenite improved somatic accumulation uniformly across the three vegetable-oil backgrounds.

Nutrient utilisation indices showed matching improvements driven by dietary trace mineral supplementation. Within the factorial treatments, sodium selenite significantly lowered the feed conversion ratio and increased the protein efficiency ratio, both achieving statistical significance at p less than 0.001. The oil regime also produced significant main effects on feed conversion ratio at p equal to 0.038 and on protein efficiency ratio at p equal to 0.049, without exhibiting a significant interaction with selenium. Feed efficiency displayed the direct reciprocal mathematical pattern of the conversion ratios. In secondary comparisons across all treatments, several selenium-supplemented 28 percent protein diets achieved feed utilisation values statistically indistinguishable from the higher-protein 32 percent reference diet, demonstrating effective nutritional sparing under the tested rearing conditions.

records.title: Canada joins NATO innovation fund, promises ‘business as usual’ with US
records.excerpt: Canada's Defence Minister David McGuinty at a summit of the so-called "Coalition of the Willing," a group of Ukraine's most significant allies and supporters, at the Chancellery in Berlin on November 19, 2026. Kenzo TRIBOUILLARD / AFP via Getty Images Stay Connected Insights & Reports How to scale agents across defense and national security agencies Presented By Google Public Sector Download Now Reclaim the mission: A federal leader’s guide to outcomes- based managed services Presented By KPMG Download Now Policy Canada joins NATO innovation fund, promises ‘business as usual’ with US But the investment is a pointed reaction to the Trump administration’s dwindling cooperation with its northern ally. Patrick Tucker | November 21, 2026 Americas Pentagon NATO Industry By Patrick Tucker Science & Technology Editor November 21, 2026 Americas Pentagon NATO Industry HALIFAX, Nova Scotia —Hours after news broke that the United States would limit defense cooperation with Canada, the Canadian government announced plans to pour 100 million Canadian dollars into a NATO defense-innovation fund. “As far as we're concerned, it's business as usual,” Defense Minister David McGuinty said when asked about the news. It was a calm reply about an extraordinary development between formerly close allies, but in one sense, it was quite true. As the Trump administration reduces its contributions to the alliance—and in some cases threatens military action against its members—they are increasing their efforts to build their own militaries and industry. The Canadian decision pushes total commitments to the NATO Innovation Fund past 1.1 billion euros. Joining the fund also makes Canadian defense startups eligible to draw upon it, giving them another source of capital and access to the fund’s network of venture capitalists. The NIF is a way to connect startups with investors and military users across the alliance to “help successful solutions reach scale,” Tarja Jaakkola, NATO’s assistant secretary general for defense industry, innovation, and armaments, said at a recent NATO conference in Izmir, Turkey. In June 2024, for instance, German ground robot maker ARX Robotics raised 9 million euros in a seed round. The NIF led the round and provided more than half the money. In April 2025, ARX raised 31 million euros in a Series A round led by HV Capital. In July, Austrian venture capital firm Speedinvest led an 11 million euro extension, bringing its Series A total to 42 million euros. But competition for the money is stiff. In April 2025, NIF partner Patrick Schneider-Sikorsky said the fund had seen “thousands” of deals and invested in about 10 companies. Canada’s pledge is a bet on collective action. The funds could have gone directly to Canadian firms, and there’s no guarantee that any of the money will come back home. There is “no pro rata in the NATO Innovation Fund. It is finding the best technologies that best address the capability needs of the alliance,” NIF President Ari Kristinn Jónsson said here on Saturday. The announcement came hours after a White House news conference at which President Donald Trump again accused Canada, the United States’ second-largest trading partner , of unfair trade practices. “For some reason they feel emboldened and we can’t let them feel that way anymore,” Trump said. Over the summer, the president imposed 50-percent tariffs on several types of Canadian products, claiming that Canada discriminates against American autos, alcohol and cheese. But, as PBS has reported , Trump’s argument “rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the U.S. president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling.” Shortly afterward, the Washington Post reported that Pentagon leaders had issued a secret memo restricting military cooperation between the United States and Canada. Canadian officials said they had learned of the memo from news reports and had yet to see it. In Halifax for the 18th Halifax International Security Forum, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said the memo was months old and limited only flag officers’ participation in social events. Rounds said it “does not impact any DoD personnel that are in Canada today. It does not impact NORAD. It does not impact NATO operations or [the Five Eyes intelligence sharing partnership]]. Does not impact general or flag officer meetings.” McGuinty pointed to more than 70 years of military cooperation between Canada and the United States. “We have Canadian vessels interdicting drug trafficking in the Caribbean, working alongside American vessels. So that cooperation remains ongoing,” he said, adding that, as far as he knew, cooperation through NORAD and intelligence-sharing agreements continued as before. “As far as we're concerned, it's business as usual. records.title: Citi Report: Fed to Raise Rates by 25 BPS in December, Cut by 75 BPS in 2027
records.excerpt: The two-year U.S. Treasury yield and the Nasdaq Index declined in tandem, as Wall Street has begun pricing in a slowdown in AI capital expenditures. In a report on November 20, Citibank U.S. economists Andrew Hollenhorst and Veronica Clark forecast that the Federal Reserve will raise rates by 25 bas... The two-year U.S. Treasury yield and the Nasdaq Index declined in tandem, as Wall Street has begun pricing in a slowdown in AI capital expenditures. In a report on November 20, Citibank U.S. economists Andrew Hollenhorst and Veronica Clark forecast that the Federal Reserve will raise rates by 25 basis points on December 9 to preserve credibility, but as inflation declines and financial conditions tighten, three cumulative 75-basis-point rate cuts are expected in the second half of 2027. Expectations of cooling AI investment are pulling down two-year U.S. Treasuries. Market pricing trends have shown subtle signs of loosening. After rising nearly 30 basis points the previous week, the two-year U.S. Treasury yield fell by approximately 15 basis points during the week of November 20, while the Nasdaq index also declined during the same period. Citibank believes that this simultaneous drop in stocks and bonds reflects investors pricing in a higher probability of slowing AI-related investments. Should AI investment cool down, overall U.S. economic growth would face significant pressure. The Federal Reserve is currently caught between two forces. Core inflation has exceeded expectations for three consecutive months, forcing officials to signal a hawkish stance with a potential 25-basis-point rate hike in December and at least one more hike by 2027. On the other side, financial conditions continue to tighten, and asymmetric downside risks to economic growth are mounting. The report states that Citigroup and most Federal Reserve officials do not believe the U.S. economy is overheating. In October, Federal Reserve Governor Kevin Warsh explicitly stated that most of his colleagues did not view the economy as running too hot, and the Fed’s goal is certainly not to throw sand in the gears of the economy or push people into unemployment. In Citi’s view, this means that the December rate hike was more about preserving the central bank’s credibility, as the Fed is extremely reluctant to raise rates high enough to burst the economic recovery. Given that AI investment has contributed a significant portion of recent U.S. real GDP growth, continued selling in U.S. equities or widening credit spreads would directly weigh on the real economy. Consumption remains temporarily resilient, but the real estate market and actual incomes are already slowing down. Observing the current state of the U.S. economy, different sectors are rapidly diverging in performance. Retail demand remains robust. In October, retail sales in the control group rose 0.6% month-over-month, continuing the resilience in consumer spending, while manufacturing output increased 0.3% month-over-month. Citi expects personal nominal income to have risen 0.4% month-over-month in October. The S&P U.S. Manufacturing PMI for November stood at 54.1, and the Services PMI at 55.2, both remaining in expansion territory. However, beneath the surface data, the seeds of a slowdown have already been sown. High energy prices and core commodity inflation have raised the cost of living, causing U.S. household real income growth to remain weak over the past several months. Citigroup expects October nominal personal spending to rise by only 0.3% month-over-month, with real consumption growth nearly stagnant after adjusting for price increases. Under pressure from high interest rates, business equipment investment and core capital goods orders are shifting from rapid expansion to a plateau. As tax incentives phase down beginning in 2027, durable goods orders are expected to slow further. The real estate market has already turned red. Burdened by high mortgage rates, single-family home building permits in the U.S. have fallen to a post-pandemic low. Citigroup expects annualized new home sales in October to drop 7.1% month-over-month to 628,000 units. With new home inventory at historically high levels, developers are cutting prices to boost sales; the weekly high-frequency median home price has turned negative year-over-year, and the lagging S&P Case-Shiller housing index is expected to weaken significantly by early 2027. The labor market remains generally stable overall, but signs of loosening have emerged. Initial and continuing claims for unemployment benefits slightly rose in mid-November. Citigroup expects monthly non-farm payroll growth to decline from an average of 80,100 jobs per month in 2026 to 50,000 per month in 2027, with the unemployment rate rising slightly from 4.2% in 2026 to 4.3% in 2027. Inflation stickiness is merely technical noise; it will decline smoothly by 2027. Another piece of the puzzle supporting Citi’s bet on a dovish shift by 2027 is the breakdown of the inflation trajectory. Citibank expects the overall PCE price index to rise 0.3% month-over-month in October and increase to 3.8% year-over-year; core PCE is projected to rise 0.27% month-over-month and edge up to 3.2% year-over-year. The report specifically notes that the elevated year-over-year core PCE data for October and November exhibit clear technical distortions. The government shutdown during the same period in 2025 caused unusually low price collection in November, lowering the comparison base. This base distortion will automatically dissipate in the December data to be released in late January 2027. Meanwhile, the factors that pushed inflation higher in 2026—such as rising energy prices, increased costs for hardware like computer memory, and higher prices for healthcare and airfare—are all temporary supply or cost shocks, and are expected to turn into deflationary or cooling forces in 2027. According to Citibank’s forecasting model, the year-over-year growth rate of U.S. core PCE is expected to peak at 3.2% in the fourth quarter of 2026, then decline quarter by quarter to 3.0%, 2.7%, 2.6%, and 2.4% in the four quarters of 2027, respectively; the year-over-year growth rate of overall CPI is projected to fall from 3.8% in the fourth quarter of 2026 to 1.8% in the fourth quarter of 2027. After a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, rate cuts are expected to resume in June 2027. By intersecting the slowing economic growth and cooling inflation trends, Citi has presented an interest rate path that differs significantly from current market pricing. As of November 20, the interest rate futures market is still pricing in further Fed rate hikes after the December increase, with rates expected to continue rising through the first half of 2027, and only slight rate cuts being priced in by the second half. Citibank directly contradicted the market consensus in its report, expecting the Fed to make its final rate hike on December 9, 2026, raising the federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points to 4.00%-4.25%, followed by a hold on further rate changes in the first half of 2027. Once the decline in inflation in the second quarter of 2027 is confirmed and the drag on GDP from tighter financial conditions becomes evident (Citigroup expects U.S. real GDP growth to slow from 2.3% in 2026 to 2.0% in 2027), the Federal Reserve will cut interest rates by 25 basis points in three separate installments on June 9, September 15, and December 8, 2027, bringing the policy rate back to the 3.25%-3.50% range by year-end. records.title: Fed monetary policy credibility caught between a rock and a hard place
records.excerpt: Fed monetary policy credibility caught between a rock and a hard place - OMFIF Skip to content Fed monetary policy credibility caught between a rock and a hard place By Mark Sobel / 20 November 2026 Falling behind on inflation amid myriad intractable challenges The Federal Reserve is rightly one of America’s most respected and revered institutions. Its leadership and staff are outstanding, and the Fed helped foster decades of price stability throughout the Great Moderation. Longer-term inflation expectations are broadly anchored. Yet, the Great Moderation is yesterday’s story. Today’s monetary policy environment confronts difficult challenges. The track record in meeting those challenges, which are often well beyond the Fed’s control, is increasingly mixed. That redounds negatively on the Fed’s credibility and reputation. Inflation The Fed states that delivering price stability is its job. But the Fed’s inflation target has been missed for six years. While roughly steady inflation of around 3% still allows households and businesses to make reliable non-distortionary decisions, the target is 2% and the difference compounds over time. Further, Americans are increasingly inflation-sensitive, especially post-pandemic and given affordability concerns. Amid low persisting inflation, the Fed developed its Flexible Average Inflation Targeting framework. The pandemic then hit, along with fiscal largesse and supply shocks. The framework soon was blamed for encouraging the Fed to continue too long with post-pandemic accommodation and took on the aura of mistakenly fighting the last war. Inflation seems increasingly entrenched, given economic resilience, artificial intelligence demand, low unemployment, energy price hikes and tariffs. One can’t dismiss the possibility of a return to more moderate inflation near the target given a squeeze on real incomes and if, for example, oil prices fall and AI demand cools. Neither can one bank on that. Monetary policy is best able to deal with demand shocks. The economy has been hit primarily by a series of supply shocks, many of which are beyond the Fed’s control. The Fed has been somewhat cautious, questioning whether the shocks are transitory and can be looked through. But demand seems increasingly buoyant and second-round effects are apparent. Financial conditions are arguably accommodative and not likely to be restrictive. Many suggest the Fed is now behind the curve. Views vary between those who believe the Fed funds rate should move 50 basis points higher and those who are calling for 100bp. There is little doubt that Doctor Fed must administer stronger medicine. Communications Clear and transparent Fed communication with markets is essential, especially as monetary policy works through the transmission of financial conditions to the real economy. That is not now happening. Chair Kevin Warsh is opposed to explicit forward guidance and believes the Fed should speak less and listen far more to market feedback, rather than vice versa. Most agree that explicit forward guidance isn’t needed except at the zero lower bound. But they also believe that, even if the Fed has been too explicit, it still should remain an important voice in shaping market expectations and that the market will seek out Fed views regardless, looking to the dot plot and Fed speeches. Thus, they argue the Fed should clearly outline its reaction function. But Warsh’s press conferences are not seen as informative, meaning his views are not shaping market direction. While Warsh’s relative silence – or interrogation of reality – may signify he does not have to voice a hawkish stance that might upset super-dovish President Donald Trump, Fed communication is now seen as having deteriorated. This is a recipe for exacerbating uncertainty and volatility across the curve as global yields are on the ascent. The White House and Treasury Technical debates about the future of the Fed’s balance sheet, whether it strays into fiscal terrain and what it means for money market management rage on. But the bigger issue is what the obvious interconnections of fiscal and monetary policy signify for the Fed and its independence. Trump has continued to plea for slashing the Fed funds rate, saving the government from a skyrocketing interest bill now in excess of 3% of gross domestic product and greater than annual US defence spending. He continues to minimise America’s inflation problem. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent – unusually – has publicly weighed in on Fed monetary policy, calling for lower rates and suggesting that higher energy prices should be looked through. In an unsuccessful effort to curb higher long-term rates, Bessent has upped the pace of Treasury buybacks. Warsh has shown that he is a defender of the Fed’s monetary policy independence and disproven those who thought he could be Trump’s ’sock puppet’. But Warsh’s task forces are not dealing with the elephant in the room: America’s massive fiscal deficits . These deficits are helping sustain demand and inflation as well as pushing up longer-term yields. Beyond suggesting US fiscal policy is unsustainable, the Fed is gun-shy in speaking about the impact of fiscal policy for demand, inflation, the yield curve and monetary policy, perhaps so as not to perturb the president. But these topics are central to the Fed’s wheelhouse and America’s health. Are fiscal and financial dominance potential threats to America? The Fed-Treasury relationship seems far less smooth than in the past, further compounding uncertainty. The Fed is caught between a rock and a hard place. It is falling behind in coping with America’s current inflation challenges after missing its inflation target for six years. The challenges are generated largely by supply shocks – energy, wars, immigration crackdowns, AI, tariffs – over which the Fed has little control. But they now appear to be feeding demand. Communications have weakened, abetting volatility. A critical administration unwilling to tame its fiscal recklessness doesn’t help. Warsh’s Fed is increasingly behind the eight ball. records.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
records.excerpt: AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. Business S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year November 20, 2026 5:11 PM ET By The Associated Press Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption Seth Wenig/AP NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. Technology Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. "The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over." Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%. Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year. The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Following October inflation readings that showed consumer prices expanding 0.4% month-over-month and producer prices rising 6.5% year-over-year, market participants aggressively priced in continued monetary tightening, with interest rate futures indicating approximately an 82% to 90% probability of an additional 25-basis-point rate hike at the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting. Benchmark Treasury yields remained under upward pressure, with the 10-year Treasury yield fluctuating between 4.91% and 5.15% after surging in prior sessions, while the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 7.28%. Compounding the macro headwinds, geopolitical friction intensified in the Middle East following maritime incidents and drone interceptions near the Strait of Hormuz, while domestic policy discourse introduced fresh uncertainty regarding potential tax liabilities and restrictions on international artificial intelligence data center construction. U.S. equities suffered severe, broad-based liquidation during the week of November 16 to November 20, 2026, culminating in the steepest weekly declines for major benchmarks in over eighteen months. The S&P 500 dropped from a weekly open of 7,561.67 to close at 6,910.39, declining 651.28 points or 8.61% for the week and officially entering technical correction territory, down 11.62% from its October 6 peak. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite sank 2,518.54 points or 10.02% to settle at 22,617.73, fully wiping out its year-to-date gains to stand down 2.7% for 2026. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 4,200.22 points or 8.02% to finish at 48,147.33, also entering correction territory, while the small-cap Russell 2000 surrendered 208.70 points or 7.48% to end at 2,581.79. Sector breadth deteriorated sharply, with Information Technology plummeting 9.62% on the week to lead all sectors lower, accompanied by heavy selling across communication services and industrials. Style rotation favored defensive value over growth, as consumer staples stood as the sole pocket of relative resilience while momentum and high-multiple growth equities experienced widespread capitulation. Key events during the week centered on pivotal central bank communication, regulatory developments, and critical corporate earnings. On November 16, Eastern Time, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh addressed the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference in San Francisco, presenting illustrative scenarios on superintelligence and cautioning that unrealized technological returns could trigger sharp valuation compression and economic drag. Simultaneously, newly released Federal Reserve meeting minutes revealed that central bank staff flagged off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing structures among technology firms as potential systemic amplifiers. Corporate earnings added further strain; Nvidia's quarterly report, its first following the departure of former chief executive Jensen Huang, disclosed 102 billion dollars in data-center lease and cloud commitments, which was subsequently compounded by reports of regulatory accounting scrutiny that drove double-digit losses across semiconductor leaders. In primary markets, the public market debut of Anthropic priced at 83 dollars per share and initially traded above 115 dollars, but fizzled into Friday with a steep drop to 88.30 dollars, failing to stem the wider tech de-risking despite solid earnings from retail anchors Walmart and Target. Capital flows and investor sentiment reflected an acute shift toward liquidity preservation and cross-asset de-leveraging. The Cboe Volatility Index spiked dramatically over the five-day period, advancing from sub-20 levels to close at 35.89, reaching as high as 37.67, its highest reading since March and signaling elevated institutional demand for downside portfolio protection. Digital assets endured forced liquidations exceeding 600 million dollars in crypto futures, with Bitcoin sliding below 60,000 dollars and U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds posting record single-day net outflows. Commodity markets also exhibited signs of cash-raising behavior, as gold fell nearly 4% on Friday to 3,539.00 dollars per ounce, extending to fresh multi-month lows alongside softening crude prices, while the U.S. dollar index strengthened as the global reserve currency absorbed defensive flows. In terms of overall market assessment, the equity complex has transitioned from an extended momentum expansion into an aggressive valuation repricing and liquidity correction phase. The core market logic has shifted from speculative multiple expansion toward an intense scrutiny of capital return timelines, exacerbated by the prospect of a more restrictive Federal Reserve interest rate trajectory. Cyclically, this phase exhibits hallmark features of mid-to-late cycle volatility, where deteriorating market breadth, regulatory scrutiny, and tightening financial conditions force a painful compression of excessive market concentration. ## Next Week’s key market drivers and Investment Outlook Upcoming events will be framed by a holiday-shortened trading schedule alongside key macroeconomic releases and corporate updates. Market participants will focus on revised third-quarter Gross Domestic Product data, October Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation figures, durable goods orders, and initial jobless claims. Investors will also parse speeches from multiple Federal Reserve officials ahead of the pre-December meeting blackout window, seeking confirmation regarding whether the central bank intends to enact a 25-basis-point or larger rate hike at the upcoming FOMC gathering. On the micro front, late-reporting retail and enterprise software earnings will provide a health check on consumer resilience and corporate software budgets heading into the year-end shopping season. Market logic projection points toward a fragile equilibrium as asset prices digest the recent breakdown in market structure. Macro conditions are likely to remain constrained by sticky wage and services inflation, keeping short-term interest rates elevated and limiting the scope for any near-term central bank accommodation. From a micro-fundamental perspective, the initial shock of technology leadership turnover and capital expenditure financing questions has driven index-level technical indicators into deeply oversold territory, which could pave the way for tactical, short-covering bounces. However, any sustainable floor in equities will require evidence of credit spread stability and clarity regarding capital-spending durability outside of circular financing channels. Strategy and allocation recommendations dictate maintaining a cautious, capital-preservation-oriented posture with disciplined risk-budgeting. records.title: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
records.excerpt: A bruising stock market sell-off continued despite a record-setting IPO by Anthropic, dashing hopes it would revive sentiment on the AI trade. The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks. The dramatic sell-off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year. Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price. Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant. With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year. The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%. The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process. While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weekslong slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices, rising interest rates, mounting corporate debt loads, stubborn inflation, supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices. The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China. “The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.” Alongside the stock sell-off, investors have increased purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China. “The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday. For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove nettlesome. Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation. “They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.” A prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth, he said. “If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.

records.title: With the Nasdaq in a Correction, Vanguard's Tech ETF Is the Fund I'd Buy Now
records.excerpt: Free Article Explore Premium Services With the Nasdaq in a Correction, Vanguard's Tech ETF Is the Fund I'd Buy Now The fund's price has slid back to its late-April level. Its earnings didn't slide with it. By Daniel Sparks – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:23PM EST Key Points The Vanguard Information Technology ETF finished at $104.99 on Nov. 19, its lowest close since May 4. Apple, Nvidia, and Microsoft made up around 47% of the fund at the end of October. The fund's holdings traded at 29.5 times earnings on Oct. 31, down from around 39 times in mid-2025. 10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Information Technology ETF › The tech sell-off that started in October has become a correction. As I write, the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -5.28% ) has dropped around 13% from its all-time closing high, hit on Oct. 6. The Vanguard Information Technology ETF ( VGT -7.00% ) has dropped even more. It finished at $104.99 on Nov. 19, its lowest close since May 4 and around 19% below its own Oct. 6 record of $129.80. That said, the fund's still up around 12% in 2026 as of this writing, counting dividends. When the fund was about 10% below its peak in late October, I didn't think it was a bargain yet. At today's price, I do. The businesses in it have kept growing their earnings as the share price dropped, and I'd be glad to pay the resulting valuation for a fund I plan to hold for years to come. Image source: The Motley Fool. Nvidia did much of the damage The fund owns 315 stocks, but a handful of them drive it. As of Oct. 31, Apple was around 18% of its assets, Nvidia ( NVDA -14.01% ) about 17%, and Microsoft about 12%. These three haven't moved in step. Apple stock is within about 2% of its record as of this writing. Nvidia , though, has fallen about 29% since Oct. 30 alone. By my math, Nvidia by itself is behind about half of the fund's 10% fall since then. The slide came with a leadership change. Nvidia said on Nov. 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. On Nov. 19, California's attorney general followed with an investigative subpoena over whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information might have gone to China, and if the company misled investors about that risk. But Nvidia's business is still booming. In the third quarter of its fiscal 2027 (the period ending Oct. 25), the company's revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion. Data center revenue climbed 110%, and non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share surged 111%. Management also forecast fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of about $130 billion. In other words, much of the fund's fall has come from investors paying less for the same chip profits, not from those profits dropping. The fund's valuation has fallen faster than its price Vanguard lists the average price-to-earnings ratio of the stocks in the fund, and that number has dropped a lot in the last year and a half. The fund's holdings traded at about 39 times earnings at the end of June 2025 and about 35 times earnings on April 30, 2026. By Sept. 30, the number was about 33 times earnings, and on Oct. 31, it was 29.5 times earnings. Granted, that last reading came before the latest 10% slide. With earnings held flat, today's price would put the ratio closer to 26 or 27 times earnings. That's a big shift for a share price that is now right back where it was in late April, when it closed around $103. By my rough math, every share of the fund now carries about a third more earnings than it did then. The gap to the broader market has shrunk, too. On Oct. 31, the stocks in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF traded at around 24 times earnings, so the tech fund's premium had fallen to about a quarter. For businesses whose profits are still growing this fast, I think the price is fair. Is it time to buy? Sure, the fund might keep sliding. A correction can become a bear market (a drop of 20% or more), and the fund is already near that mark. And with three stocks making up almost half of its assets, a tough patch for just one of them can drag on the whole fund. VGT - Vanguard Information Technology ETF $97.64 -$7.35 (-7.00%) NYSEMKT · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26 Key data points AUM $145.10B Dividend yield 1.83% Expense ratio 0.09% Top holdings AAPL 17.68% NVDA 16.92% MSFT 12.19% But a long holding period changes how much a fall like this matters. After all, this year has already shown how quickly the mood can turn. The fund closed at around $84 on March 30 (adjusted for its 8-for-1 stock split in April), and it then rose about 55% to its Oct. 6 high in just over six months. No one knows where this sell-off stops. But an investor planning to hold for five or 10 years is largely buying the earnings these companies produce in that stretch. And those earnings seem to have kept climbing through both of this year's sell-offs. Is the fund worth buying at around $105 a share? I think so. Its valuation has fallen far more than its price, and its largest companies are still growing. I'd buy the fund now, maybe in a few chunks over the coming months, because the sell-off might go further first.
